question: What is mandatory before salivary-gland cancer is managed?

options.B: Clinical examination and pathological confirmation [IV, A]
options.D: Open biopsy of every parotid mass

correctAnswerText: Clinical examination and pathological confirmation [IV, A]
explanation: Clinical examination and pathological confirmation are mandatory, graded [IV, A] [1].
sourceArticle: Salivary gland cancer: ESMO–European Reference Network on Rare Adult Solid Cancers (EURACAN) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up

question: If fine-needle aspiration is non-diagnostic, the next step is:

options.A: Open biopsy of the parotid as the preferred next step
options.C: Observation for a year with no further sampling

explanation: Fine-needle aspiration is used for screening. If it is inadequate, core needle biopsy is an accepted next step [III, A]. Open biopsy of a major gland is avoided [1].
sourceArticle: Salivary gland cancer: ESMO–European Reference Network on Rare Adult Solid Cancers (EURACAN) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up

question: Which imaging does ESMO prefer when malignancy is suspected?

options.A: Ultrasound alone and no further imaging
options.E: Contrast CT for every patient, including those who can have MRI

explanation: When malignancy is suspected, MRI is the preferred imaging modality [IV, A]. Contrast CT is mostly limited to patients who cannot have MRI [1].
sourceArticle: Salivary gland cancer: ESMO–European Reference Network on Rare Adult Solid Cancers (EURACAN) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up

question: How does preoperative facial-nerve function change the operation?

options.B: Always preserve it, even if it is already paralysed
options.C: The nerve is not relevant to parotid surgery
options.D: Radiotherapy replaces any decision about the nerve
options.E: Try to preserve the nerve if there is no paralysis; sacrifice it if paralysis is already present

correctAnswerText: Try to preserve the nerve if there is no paralysis; sacrifice it if paralysis is already present
explanation: It is logical to try to preserve the facial nerve when there is no preoperative paralysis, and to sacrifice it when paralysis is already present [1].
sourceArticle: Salivary gland cancer: ESMO–European Reference Network on Rare Adult Solid Cancers (EURACAN) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up

question: Postoperative radiotherapy to the primary site is recommended for:

options.A: T3–T4 disease, high or intermediate grade, close or incomplete margins, or perineural growth
options.D: T1 low-grade tumours with wide margins and no other risk feature
options.E: Replacement of surgery in every patient

correctAnswerText: T3–T4 disease, high or intermediate grade, close or incomplete margins, or perineural growth
explanation: Postoperative radiotherapy is recommended for T3–T4 disease, high or intermediate grade, close or incomplete margins, and perineural growth. Adding chemotherapy in the cited database analysis did not improve survival [1].
sourceArticle: Salivary gland cancer: ESMO–European Reference Network on Rare Adult Solid Cancers (EURACAN) Clinical Practice Guideline for diagnosis, treatment and follow-up
